title: Loneliness
hookLine: lunch alone, and the Buddha and an elephant who both left the crowd
tomorrow: why would a wish for all beings mention the ones you never see?

cards: Lunch alone, earbuds in, scrolling so nobody can see there's nobody to talk to. The Buddha knew a crowd that had gone sour.
At Kosambi, tradition tells, his monks fell into a quarrel so bitter they wouldn't listen even to him. He tried, more than once, to make peace. They told him, in effect, to leave it to them.
So he did something surprising. He set out alone, no attendant, no word to anyone, and walked into the forest of Parileyyaka.
And in that same forest, a great bull elephant had just done the same thing: walked away from his herd.

teach.h: AN ELEPHANT TIRED OF THE HERD.
teach.b: The Udana tells the elephant's side. He was tired of being jostled, of trampled grass and water churned to mud by the herd. So he left, and found the Buddha under a tree.
The commentaries add that he brought him water and kept the ground clear.
Two beings who had both had enough of the crowd, at ease together in the quiet. The verse says their minds agreed.
The Dhammapada says something close: if you can't find a wise companion, walk alone, like an elephant in the forest. Solitude, in this telling, isn't a failure. It can be rest.
An empty room after a long, loud week can feel like a drink of cold water. But here's the cliffhanger answered.
He didn't stay. The Vinaya tells that the quarreling monks, embarrassed when lay people stopped supporting them, came to ask forgiveness, and the community was mended.

And elsewhere, when Ananda suggests that good friendship is half of the holy life, the Buddha corrects him: not half, the whole of it. So the forest was a rest stop, not a home. Being alone can heal a tired mind.
Loneliness is a different ache, and the path's answer to it is sangha: people walking the same way.

how: Buddhists balance solitary practice with sangha: some take retreats alone or in silence, and come back to practice with a group at a temple, center or home.

o: an ache solitude can rest, and community answers
proof that you're further along the path than others
a feeling Buddhists are taught to deny completely

games.q: the forest and the return — tap the pairs.
p: where the monks fell into a quarrel
the forest where the Buddha went alone
tired of the herd, at ease with him
not half the holy life, the whole

s: the Buddha taught that the ideal life is to be alone, always
he rested in the forest, then went back; good friendship is the whole of the holy life.
an elephant who left his herd kept the Buddha company in the forest
the Udana tells the elephant's side; the commentaries add that he brought water.

games.q: you moved to a new city a month ago. weekends alone felt peaceful at first; now they feel heavy. what does the forest story suggest?
o: lean in; solitude is the higher path, and the heaviness will pass.
the rest did its work. now look for a group to walk with.
fill every weekend with plans so the alone feeling never comes back.
games.why: the Buddha rested in the forest, then returned. alone can heal; loneliness is an ache the path answers with sangha.

practice: First, sit with being alone for a minute, phone face down, like the elephant at the river: nothing to perform for anyone.
Then let one person come to mind, someone you haven't heard from in a while, someone who might be eating lunch alone too, and plan the first words you'd send them.

wordCard.voice: Loneliness: the ache the forest can rest but can't cure. The Buddha's answer was solitude for a while, then sangha.

orig.note: Pali: community; the people who walk the path together.

carryVoice: Keep this close: alone, then together, in that order and not forever. Three of six on friends and community.

sources.ref: Udana 4.5 (Naga Sutta: the Buddha leaves Kosambi alone for Parileyyaka; the bull elephant weary of the herd; their minds agree in solitude)
Vinaya, Mahavagga X (the Kosambi quarrel and its reconciliation)
Dhammapada 329 (if one finds no prudent companion, walk alone, like an elephant in the forest)
Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (Upaddha Sutta: good friendship is not half but the whole of the holy life)
